summary: Take control of your hours with priorities, time-blocking and planned rest.
goals: Sort tasks by urgency and importance using the Eisenhower matrix
Build a one-week time-block schedule that includes study, practice and rest
Say a polite 'no' to protect your focus
idea: Almost nobody runs out of hours; what runs out is deliberate decisions about how those hours are used. 'I don't have time' often means 'I have not decided this matters more than what currently fills my time'. That sentence puts the choice back in your hands.

Time management is really priority management. A to-do list shows what you want to do; a calendar shows what you will do. Putting tasks into real time blocks forces honesty about how long things take and where they fit, and planned rest keeps you from burning out.
oneLine: Decide your priorities on purpose, give them a time block, and schedule rest as part of the plan.
steps: Prioritise: sort tasks into four boxes: Urgent and Important (do now), Important not Urgent (schedule), Urgent not Important (delegate or shorten), Neither (drop)
Block: put the important tasks on a calendar with a start and end time, for example 'Homework 4:00 to 5:00 pm, phone in another room'
Protect: say no kindly to things that steal your blocks: 'I cannot join now, I am studying until 5. Can we meet after?'
Review: spend 15 minutes every Sunday evening adjusting next week's blocks based on what really happened
scenarioSetup: Temi has football on Tuesdays and Thursdays, tutorials on Wednesdays, a big Biology test in nine days and a group project due Friday. Her evenings disappear into WhatsApp and TikTok.
scenarioWrong: She writes an enormous to-do list, panics on Thursday night, copies part of the project from a friend and studies for Biology at midnight.
scenarioBetter: Sort: Biology test and project are Important (and soon Urgent); TikTok is Neither
Block: Mon, Wed, Fri 5 to 6 pm Biology; Tue and Thu 7 to 7:45 pm project; Saturday morning rest and sport
Protect: tell friends, 'I am offline from 5 to 6, message me after'
Review: on Sunday, move any missed block to the next day instead of dropping it
mistakes: Mistake: planning every minute with no slack. Fix: Leave 20 per cent of your day flexible for surprises.
Mistake: leaving rest out. Fix: Schedule sleep, meals and play as real blocks.
Mistake: starting with the hardest task at your lowest-energy time. Fix: Do demanding work in your best focus hours.
lab: (5 min) List everything on your plate this week
(10 min) Sort it into the Eisenhower matrix
(10 min) Build a one-week time-block schedule on paper or a phone calendar
(5 min) Practise saying 'no' to a partner using the 'I cannot now, but I can later' form
reflect: What eats my time without my noticing?
Which important-but-not-urgent task do I keep postponing?
What would I do with one extra protected hour a day?
takeaways: A calendar is more honest than a to-do list
challenge: Build a one-week time-block schedule and follow it for seven days. On Sunday, note which blocks worked and which did not, and adjust. Add the first and the adjusted schedules to your portfolio.

check.q: In the Eisenhower matrix, where do 'important but not urgent' tasks belong?
o: Do them immediately in a panic

check.q: Why is time-blocking often better than a long to-do list?
o: It forces you to fit tasks into real time and be honest about how long they take
It removes the need to rest

check.q: Your friends invite you out during your study block. What is the best response?
o: Say yes and study later at midnight
Say, 'I am studying until 5, can we meet after?'

summary: Notice, name and manage your own emotions before they manage you.
goals: Name at least ten different emotions beyond 'happy', 'sad' and 'angry'
Use Pause, Label, Choose when an emotion is strong
Tell the difference between an emotion and the action you choose
idea: Emotional intelligence is the ability to notice your own emotions, understand what causes them and choose how to respond. Self-awareness is its foundation: you cannot manage what you cannot name. Emotions are not good or bad; they are signals, like a dashboard light, telling you something needs attention.

When a feeling is strong, the thinking part of the brain gets harder to reach. Research on 'affect labelling' suggests that simply putting a precise word to a feeling can reduce its intensity. 'I feel disrespected' gives you something to work with in a way that 'I am just angry' does not.
oneLine: Name it to tame it: a precise word for the feeling gives you room to choose your response.
steps: Pause: stop for one slow breath before you speak or act; notice where you feel it in your body
Label: name the feeling precisely, such as 'embarrassed', 'jealous' or 'overwhelmed', using an emotion wheel if needed
Choose: ask, 'What do I need right now, and what is the most helpful thing I can do?' Options include walking away, asking for help or speaking calmly
Review: later, ask what the feeling was trying to tell you
scenarioSetup: Dayo's team loses a football match because of a teammate's mistake. In the changing room, someone laughs. Dayo feels hot in the face and clenches his fists.
scenarioWrong: Without pausing, he shouts at the teammate, throws his bag and is dropped from the next game. His emotion made the decision.
scenarioBetter: Pause: one deep breath; notice the heat in the face
Label: 'I am embarrassed and disappointed, and I feel disrespected by the laughing'
Choose: step outside for two minutes, then say calmly, 'I was upset about the loss. Let us work on that pass in training.'
mistakes: Mistake: believing you should never feel anger or fear. Fix: All emotions are information; manage the action, not the feeling.
Mistake: using one word like 'fine' for everything. Fix: Build a wider emotion vocabulary.
Mistake: acting first, thinking later. Fix: Make the one-breath pause a habit.
lab: (5 min) Look at an emotion wheel and write ten feelings you have had this month
(10 min) Recall a recent strong emotion and write the situation, body signals, label and what you did
(10 min) Role-play a heated moment in pairs, practising Pause, Label, Choose out loud
(5 min) Agree a private signal that reminds you to pause
reflect: Where in my body do I feel anger, fear and excitement?
Which emotion do I find hardest to admit, and why?
How would my last argument have changed with a ten-second pause?
takeaways: A precise word reduces a feeling's power
The gap between feeling and action is where you choose
challenge: Keep a three-day Emotion Log: each evening, write the strongest feeling of the day, its trigger, its precise name and what you did. Circle one moment when you could have paused. Add the log to your portfolio.

check.q: What is the main benefit of labelling an emotion precisely?
o: It helps you understand it and choose a response
It lets others guess your thoughts

check.q: In Pause, Label, Choose, what comes first?

o: You made me angry, so I shouted
I feel embarrassed and I need a minute before I answer
I will never feel this way again

summary: Understand other people's feelings and build stronger relationships through empathy.
goals: Tell cognitive empathy from sympathy and explain why empathy is a skill you can practise
Use See, Ask, Reflect Back to understand a friend's feelings
Offer support in a way the other person actually wants
idea: Empathy is understanding what another person feels and why, from their point of view. It is different from sympathy, which is feeling sorry for someone from the outside, and different from agreeing, which you can do without understanding. Empathy is a skill: we get better at it by paying attention, asking and checking.

Strong relationships are built on feeling understood. Teams, friendships and families all work better when people feel their feelings are taken seriously. The good news is that empathy does not need long speeches; one accurate sentence like 'It sounds like you felt left out' can change a conversation.
oneLine: Empathy: see the situation through the other person's eyes, check you have understood, and then help in the way they want.
steps: See: notice the face, voice, body language and what changed in their behaviour
Ask: use open questions such as 'How are you feeling about this?' or 'What is the hardest part?'
Reflect back: say what you heard in your own words, 'It sounds like you are disappointed because you worked hard on this'
Offer: ask what would help, 'Do you want advice, or do you just want me to listen?'
scenarioSetup: Ngozi has been quiet for two days. When her friend Hauwa asks what is wrong, she says, 'Nothing, I am fine.' Her best friend did not invite her to a birthday party.
scenarioWrong: Hauwa says, 'Do not be silly, it is only a party,' and moves on. Ngozi feels even more alone and stops talking.
scenarioBetter: See: Hauwa notices Ngozi eating alone and avoiding eye contact
Ask: 'You seem quiet lately. I am here if you want to talk about anything.'
Reflect back: 'It sounds like being left out really hurt.'
Offer: 'Do you want me to sit with you, or would you like ideas for what to do next?'
mistakes: Mistake: rushing to fix or give advice. Fix: Listen first and ask if advice is wanted.
Mistake: comparing ('That is nothing, I once...'). Fix: Keep the focus on their experience.
Mistake: assuming you know how they feel. Fix: Check by asking and reflecting back.
lab: (5 min) Read three short scenarios and write what each person might be feeling
(10 min) In pairs, one person shares a mild frustration while the other uses See, Ask, Reflect Back
(5 min) Swap roles
(5 min) Discuss: what did the reflection feel like to receive?
reflect: When did someone understand me really well, and what did they do?
Who in my life needs me to listen better right now?
Do I tend to fix, compare or listen, and what could I try instead?
takeaways: Empathy is a practised skill, not a personality type
Reflecting back shows you are listening
Ask what help is wanted before offering it
challenge: Choose one person and have a five-minute conversation using See, Ask, Reflect Back, with no advice unless asked. Afterwards write what you learned about them and about yourself, and add it to your portfolio.

o: Understanding how someone feels from their point of view

check.q: Which is a good reflecting-back sentence?
o: It sounds like you felt left out, and that hurt
At least it is not a big problem
I felt worse than that once

check.q: Before offering advice to a friend who is upset, the best step is to:
o: Ask whether they want advice or just someone to listen

summary: Design small daily habits that stick using cues, routines, rewards and 'tiny starts'.
goals: Explain the cue, routine, reward loop behind any habit
Design one tiny habit and attach it to something you already do
Plan for a missed day so one slip does not become a spiral
idea: A habit is a behaviour repeated so often that it becomes almost automatic. Habits follow a loop: a cue (a trigger), a routine (the action) and a reward (the benefit). A UCL study found it took people an average of 66 days for a new behaviour to become automatic, but the range was huge, from 18 to 254 days, so patience matters more than perfection.

The secret to starting is to shrink the habit until it is almost too small to fail, such as one push-up or reading one page, and to attach it to something you already do. This is called habit stacking: 'After I brush my teeth, I will read one page.' Success feels good, and that feeling helps the habit stick.
oneLine: Make it tiny, attach it to a cue, reward yourself, and never miss twice in a row.
steps: Choose one tiny habit that supports a goal, such as 'write one sentence in my journal'
Cue: attach it to an existing habit, 'After I pour my morning tea...'
Routine: do the tiny version (it must take under two minutes); you may do more, but you must do the tiny one
Reward: celebrate straight away with a tick on a tracker, a smile, or 'Yes!'; and follow the rule 'never miss twice'
scenarioSetup: Adaeze wants to read more. She promises herself one hour every night, but after a tiring day she skips it, feels guilty and gives up after four days.
scenarioWrong: The habit is too big, has no cue and has no reward except guilt when it fails.
scenarioBetter: Attach it: 'After I get into bed, I read one page'
Reward: tick a calendar box and enjoy the streak
Plan for slips: 'If I miss a day, I read two pages the next night, but I never skip twice.'
mistakes: Mistake: starting with five new habits. Fix: Build one at a time.
Mistake: relying on motivation. Fix: Rely on cues and environment, like leaving your book on your pillow.
Mistake: giving up after one missed day. Fix: Use the 'never miss twice' rule.
lab: (5 min) Choose one habit that would help a goal
(5 min) Shrink it to a two-minute version
(10 min) Write the habit stack: 'After I ____, I will ____'
(10 min) Design a simple tracker and a reward; share your plan with a partner who will check in
reflect: Which of my current habits help me most, and which hurt?
What cue could I attach my new habit to?
What do I say to myself when I miss a day?
takeaways: Habits run on cue, routine and reward
challenge: Run your tiny habit for 14 days using a tracker. At the end, write what helped, what got in the way and how you will adjust. Add the tracker to your portfolio; it feeds your Quarter 1 Capstone.

check.q: What are the three parts of the habit loop?
Why make a new habit tiny?
o: So it is easy to start and hard to fail
Because small habits do not matter

check.q: You miss your habit on Monday. What does 'never miss twice' tell you to do?
o: Do it on Tuesday, even if only the tiny version

summary: Bounce back from failure by treating it as information, getting support and choosing a next step.
goals: Explain resilience as a set of skills, not a trait you are born with
Use Feel, Learn, Support, Next Step after a setback
Write a 'failure resume' that turns setbacks into lessons
idea: Resilience is the ability to recover and keep growing after a setback. It is not about being tough or hiding pain; resilient people feel disappointment too. What differs is what they do next: they allow the feeling, find the lesson, lean on other people and take one small step forward.

Everyone who has achieved something has a hidden list of failures: rejected applications, lost matches, projects that flopped. Seeing failure as a normal part of learning removes much of its sting. The question shifts from 'What is wrong with me?' to 'What can this teach me?'
oneLine: Resilience: feel it, learn from it, ask for support, then take one small next step.
steps: Feel: allow the disappointment for a short, set time instead of pretending it is not there
Learn: ask, 'What happened? What was in my control? What would I do differently?'
Support: tell one trusted person; talking shrinks the problem and brings ideas
Next step: choose one small, specific action within 24 hours, such as booking a retake or asking for feedback
scenarioSetup: Seun submits a science fair project and does not make the finals. His classmates celebrate the winners while he sits quietly, thinking, 'I wasted three months.'
scenarioWrong: He deletes the project and refuses to enter again, so he never discovers that the judges only wanted a clearer explanation of his results.
scenarioBetter: Feel: take the evening to be disappointed, then stop
Learn: ask a judge for feedback; he learns his data was good but his explanation was confusing
Support: talk to his teacher and a friend who entered last year
Next step: redo the slides this week and enter the regional fair
mistakes: Mistake: bottling feelings up. Fix: Name the emotion and tell someone you trust.
Mistake: blaming only yourself or only others. Fix: Separate what you controlled from what you did not.
Mistake: hiding failure. Fix: Share what you learned; it helps others too.
lab: (5 min) Write one setback from the last year
(10 min) Run Feel, Learn, Support, Next Step on it in writing
(10 min) Start a 'Failure Resume': three failures, what each taught you, and what you did next
(5 min) Share one lesson with a partner
reflect: Which setback taught me the most, and how do I know?
Who do I turn to when things go wrong, and who should I add?
What is one thing I avoid because I fear failing at it?
takeaways: One small next step restarts momentum
challenge: Complete your Failure Resume with at least three entries (what happened, what you learned, what you did next). Choose one current setback and take your next step. Add the resume to your portfolio.

o: Recovering and learning after a setback

check.q: After a failure, what does 'Support' in Feel, Learn, Support, Next Step mean?

o: It shows that setbacks are normal and turns them into lessons
